title: What a data system is: records, derived data and two kinds of work
goal: By the end you can say what a database, an index, a cache, a queue and a batch job are each for, tell a system of record from the data derived from it and rebuild one from the other, and sort any question about your data into operational or analytical work.

warmup.q: Your payments service stores every payment in its database. Support staff find payments through a separate search index (by the last four digits of the card, by customer email). One night the search index is corrupted and has to be deleted. What have you lost?
options: Every payment made since the index was last backed up
Nothing that can't be rebuilt: read every payment from the database and index it again
The payments themselves, because the index held the only copy of the search fields
Only the payments that were being indexed when it broke
warmup.why: The index holds nothing of its own. Every entry in it was computed from a payment in the database, so you can delete it and compute it again. That makes it derived data, and the database is the system of record. Rebuilding takes time, because it reads every payment once, and searches are slow or unavailable until it's done, but no fact is gone. The first and last options are the trap for anyone who thinks of the index as storage: it only ever held copies.

sections.h: One file of payments, and where it stops being enough
sections.body:
Here is the smallest payments service that could work. Every time a card payment goes through, it adds one line to the end of a file called `payments.log`:

```text
pay-0000001 m-cafe 2026-03-02 CAPTURED 47800
```

That line is a **record**: one fact the system keeps. Here it says that payment `pay-0000001`, taken by the merchant `m-cafe` on 2 March 2026, captured 478.00 (amounts are in cents, so sums stay exact). The first field is the record's key, the value you look it up by. Writing only at the end of a file is simple and fast, and when the service restarts, every payment is still there. A store that survives restarts and crashes is called durable.

For a week this is enough. Then support staff need to answer a customer: what happened to payment `pay-0412233`? The only way to find a line is to read the file from the top until it turns up. With a million payments the file is 46 MB, and finding the last one took 44 ms in this lesson's demo, with the whole file already in memory. If support and the merchants together ask 200 such questions a second, that is almost 9 seconds of reading for every second that passes. The service can't keep up.

The fix is an **index**: a lookup table from a key to where its record lives. Read the file once, note the byte position where each payment's line starts, and keep that in a hash map. A lookup is now one map access and one short read, about a microsecond in the demo, tens of thousands of times faster. The price is memory for the map, a little extra work on every write, and a map that is gone after a restart and has to be built again from the file.

Next, merchants get a dashboard that shows what they took today. Working that out means adding up every one of the merchant's lines from today. Two thousand merchants refreshing every 10 seconds ask the same question over and over, and the answer rarely changes. So you keep each answer and hand it out until a new payment for that merchant arrives. That is a **cache**: a saved copy of an answer that was expensive to compute.

After each payment the service also emails a receipt, and the email provider sometimes takes 800 ms to reply. The card terminal shouldn't wait for that. So the service writes a job, "send the receipt for `pay-0000001`", into a **queue**, a list of work waiting to be done, and answers the terminal at once. A separate worker takes jobs off the queue and does them. If the email provider is down for ten minutes, the jobs wait in the queue and none is lost.

At night, settlement runs: every merchant is paid what they took that day, minus refunds and fees. That is one program that reads all of yesterday's payments from start to end and writes one payout per merchant. A program that processes a large, fixed batch of input, usually on a schedule, is a **batch job**.

Put the pieces together and you have a data system: a few tools, each built for one kind of access, joined up by your code. Real products fill each role. PostgreSQL or Oracle is the database (and builds its own indexes), Redis is a common cache, Kafka or RabbitMQ carries queues, and Spark or a plain scheduled program runs batch jobs. When an application's hardest problems are about its data (how much there is, how fast it changes, how to keep the copies in step when machines fail) rather than about computing, it is called data-intensive, and every payments system is one.

try.title: Scan a file, then use an index
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the demo below. It writes one million payments to a temporary file, one line each, then finds the last one twice: by reading the file from the top, and through an index it builds in one pass.
Predict before you run it: how many times faster will the indexed lookup be? 10? 1,000? More?
Run it again with `-Pargs=5000000` at the end of the command, for five million payments. Before you look, say which number will grow and which will stay the same.

code.title: OneFileDemo.kt (excerpt)

try.expect:
```text
file: 1,000,000 payments, 45.6 MB
pay-0000001 m-cafe 2026-03-02 CAPTURED 47800
scan:   found pay-1000000 after reading every line: 44 ms
index:  built for 1,000,000 ids in 104 ms
lookup: pay-1000000 m-cafe 2026-03-02 CAPTURED 28700 in 1.1 µs each (average of 10,000)
speed-up: about 39,362x
```

With `-Pargs=5000000`:

```text
file: 5,000,000 payments, 227.9 MB
scan:   found pay-5000000 after reading every line: 252 ms
index:  built for 5,000,000 ids in 730 ms
lookup: pay-5000000 m-books 2026-03-02 CAPTURED 8000 in 1.4 µs each (average of 10,000)
```

(output trimmed). The scan grows with the file, about 5 times for 5 times the payments, because it reads every line. The lookup stays near a microsecond whatever the size, because it touches one line. Your numbers depend on your machine, and they vary from run to run. The file fits in memory here (the kernel keeps recently used file data in RAM, which the Operating systems track explains), so a scan from a real disk would be slower still. Building the index costs a full scan too, once: that's the price of a restart.

sections.h: Systems of record and derived data
sections.body:
Look at the figure again and ask of each box: if I deleted it, could I get it back? The index: yes, read the log and build it again. The cache: yes, and it refills by itself as people ask. Last night's payouts: yes, run the batch job again over the same day of payments. The log: no. If `payments.log` is gone, nothing in the system knows that `pay-0000001` ever happened.

That question splits all data into two kinds. A **system of record**, also called the source of truth, holds the authoritative version of each fact. A new fact is written there first, each fact appears there once, and when anything else disagrees with it, the system of record is right by definition. **Derived data** is everything computed from it: indexes, caches, totals, search indexes, reports, a fraud model trained on last year's payments. It is redundant on purpose, and it can always be thrown away and computed again.

Why keep copies at all? Because each copy makes one kind of read fast. The log is good at appending and at being read from start to end. Each derived view reshapes the same facts for one question: by payment id, by merchant and day, by card number. The general name for a stored answer is a **materialized view**: the result of a query, kept so the query doesn't have to run again. "Net takings per merchant per day" is a materialized view of the log.

Copies cost something too. A derived view can be stale (it hasn't seen the newest record yet) or wrong (a bug, a lost update). The Try it below makes one go stale on purpose. Two habits keep this manageable. Write to the system of record first and update the views second, so that a crash in between leaves a view behind the truth, never ahead of it. And keep the record complete and in its original order, so that any view can be rebuilt by replaying the record from the start.

Being a system of record is a role, not a product. A PostgreSQL table is the source of truth for payments in one company and a read-only reporting copy in another. A Kafka topic can be the truth that databases are built from; the Stream processing track builds exactly that. When you look at an architecture, ask of every store whether this is where the fact is decided or a copy of it. Most of this course is about making fast copies and keeping them in step with the truth: the Caching track, the Replication track and all of Part IV.

refs.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 1 (systems of record and derived data)

sections.h: Two kinds of work: operational and analytical
sections.body:
Here are two questions about the same payments.

The checkout code asks: is payment `pay-0412233` captured? It asks thousands of times a second, needs the answer in a few milliseconds, and each answer touches one record, found by its key. The questions are fixed in advance, written into the application. Its writes have the same shape: insert one payment, update one status.

An analyst asks: what share of payments were refunded, per merchant category, per week, over the last two years? She asks a few times a day, a little differently each time, and is happy to wait seconds or minutes. The answer touches every payment from two years, possibly hundreds of millions of records, but reads only three fields of each.

The first is **operational** work, usually called OLTP, online transaction processing. (Here a transaction means a business event such as a sale. The Transactions track gives the word its stricter database meaning.) The second is **analytical** work, OLAP, online analytical processing. They differ on almost every axis:

| | Operational (OLTP) | Analytical (OLAP) |
|---|---|---|
| Who asks | your application code | analysts, reports, data scientists |
| Records per question | one or a few, by key | millions, by scanning |
| Answer needed in | milliseconds | seconds to minutes |
| The questions | fixed, written into the code | new ones every day |
| The data describes | the latest state | the history of events |
| Typical size | gigabytes to terabytes | terabytes to petabytes |
| Writes | one record at a time | bulk loads or event streams |

Everyone starts by running the analyst's question on the operational database, and it breaks for a plain reason. The scan reads every row, so while it runs it competes for disk, memory and CPU with checkout's lookups, and checkout slows down for everybody. The layout also suits only one kind of work. An operational database stores all of a payment's fields together, so fetching one payment is one read. The analyst's question needs three fields from every payment and has to drag the other twenty through memory with them. An analytical store does the opposite and keeps each field, each column, together, so a scan reads only the columns it needs.

The Try it shows both sides: the point lookup takes tens of nanoseconds, the analytical question touches two million rows, and storing the three fields it needs as columns makes it faster even in memory. On disk the gap is far larger; the Storage engines track measures it in its lesson on column stores.

Some products, called HTAP (hybrid transactional and analytical processing), run both kinds of work in one system, usually with two engines inside. They suit cases such as a fraud check that needs aggregates over very fresh data. They don't remove the need for a separate analytical copy, because a company has many operational databases and wants one place to analyze all of them together.

try.title: One row against two million
steps: Run the demo below from the `labs` folder. It builds two million payments in memory twice: as one object per payment (rows) and as one array per field (columns).
Predict the ratio between the analytical question's time and one lookup. A thousand? A million?
Look at the two analytical times. Both read every payment. What does the column version not have to read?

code.title: TwoKindsDemo.kt (excerpt)

try.expect:
```text
operational: payment 1234567 -> merchant 2382, 204.00, refunded=false
             1 row touched, about 42 ns per lookup (average of 100,000)
analytical:  refund rate per category per week, 8 categories x 104 weeks
             2,000,000 rows touched
             row layout    5.7 ms
             column layout 3.5 ms
             e.g. category 2, week 52: 4.7% of 2,405 payments refunded
```

The lookup time moved between about 20 and 60 ns over three runs on one laptop; the scans moved by about 1 ms. The shape doesn't change: the analytical question does 2 million times the work of the operational one. Each row object here carries 17 fields, about 110 bytes, and the question needs 3 of them, 9 bytes per payment. The column layout reads only those bytes, which is why it wins even though everything is already in RAM. A row store on disk has to read the whole row from storage, so there the gap grows to many times this.

sections.h: Where the analytical copy lives: warehouses, lakes and lakehouses
sections.body:
So the analytical work moves to its own copy of the data. Where that copy lives, and in what format, has had three answers.

The first, from the late 1980s and early 1990s, is the **data warehouse**: a separate database built for analytical queries, holding a read-only copy of the data from all the operational systems. A payments company might run a payments database, a merchant onboarding database, a fraud-case tool and a customer-support system. The warehouse holds all of them, reshaped into tables that suit analysis. Getting the data there is ETL: extract from each source, transform into the warehouse's shape, load. When the transform runs inside the warehouse after loading, it's called ELT. A warehouse is derived data: one very large materialized view of many systems of record, usually a few hours or a day behind them.

The second answer is the **data lake**. It grew in the 2000s with Hadoop, open-source software for storing and processing files across many machines, and moved to cloud object storage from about 2015. Object storage is a service such as Amazon S3 that stores files, called objects, by name, cheaply and durably, and is read in large chunks. A lake holds files in any format, with no schema (a declared structure: which fields, of which types) checked when they are written: raw JSON events, CSV exports, Parquet files (a column-oriented file format), images. Whoever reads them decides what they mean. That's cheap and flexible, and data scientists get the raw data a warehouse would have cleaned away. But a folder of files is not a table. Two jobs writing at once can leave a reader seeing half of an update, you can't change one row in place, and nobody can say which files make up the current version. Many companies ended up running both, a lake for raw data and a warehouse loaded from it: two copies that drift apart.

The third answer is the **lakehouse**, named in a 2021 paper by Armbrust, Ghodsi, Xin and Zaharia: warehouse behaviour on lake storage. The data stays in open file formats such as Parquet on object storage. An open table format such as Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake adds metadata files that list exactly which data files make up each version of a table. A commit writes new data files, then swaps one pointer to a new metadata file in a single atomic step, so a reader sees the old version or the new one, never a mix. That brings transactions, schemas and time travel (reading the table as it was yesterday), and several engines (Spark, Trino, DuckDB) can read the same table. The Batch processing track builds one with Iceberg.

All three hold derived data at large scale; a payment is still decided in the operational systems they copy from.

try.title: Sort a payments company's stores
steps: For each store below, write two words: system of record or derived, and operational or analytical.

1. The `payments` table in PostgreSQL that checkout writes to. 2. A Redis cache of merchant balances for the dashboard. 3. An OpenSearch index support uses to find payments by the last four digits of a card. 4. A nightly Iceberg table of every payment, for analysts. 5. A Kafka topic `payment-events` that the payments service writes to first, and from which the ledger database is built. 6. A fraud model trained on last year's chargebacks. 7. CSV exports in S3 that finance keeps just in case.
For each one you marked derived, name the source you would rebuild it from.
try.expect:
1. The `payments` table checkout writes to: system of record, operational.
2. The Redis cache of merchant balances: derived, operational. It's rebuilt from the ledger and serves the dashboard's fast reads.
3. The OpenSearch index support uses: derived, operational. Delete it and you re-index from the payments table.
4. The nightly Iceberg table for analysts: derived, analytical.
5. The `payment-events` topic: system of record, because the event is written there first and the ledger database is built from it. In a company that commits to the database first and copies changes into Kafka, the same topic would be derived. The role comes from the data flow, not from the product.
6. The fraud model: derived (from historical chargebacks), even though it is used on the operational path to score each payment.
7. The CSV exports in S3: derived, analytical. They are a small, unmanaged data lake: nobody can say which files are current.

If you put the Redis cache under "system of record" because the dashboard reads only from it, look at the stepper again: whatever the dashboard reads, the cache can be thrown away and rebuilt from the ledger.

sections.h: How the rest of this course is laid out
sections.body:
Every lesson from here on zooms into part of the picture you have just built: a record of facts, the copies derived from it, and the two kinds of work that read them. The course has four parts.

| Part | Tracks | The question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| I. Foundations | What data systems are for (this track), Computer networking, Operating systems | What do we ask of a data system, and what do the network and the kernel under every one of them do? |
| II. Data on one machine | The relational model and SQL; Data models beyond tables; Storage engines and query execution; Caching and in-memory data; Encoding, APIs and workflows | How does one server model, store, find, cache and encode data? |
| III. Data across machines | Replication; Partitioning; Transactions; Faults, time and truth; Consistency and consensus | What changes when copies live on many machines that fail on their own? |
| IV. Moving and deriving data | Messaging and logs; Stream processing; Batch processing and analytics; Derived data and doing right | How does data flow from systems of record into everything derived from them, and how do you keep that honest? |

The rest of this track sets up the words the whole course uses to judge a design. Lesson 2 measures speed: response time, percentiles, and why the slowest 1% of requests matters more than the average. Lesson 3 is about faults: how often hardware breaks, why one software bug can take down every machine at once, and how teams learn from outages. Lesson 4 describes load, with a social network's home timeline as the case study. Lesson 5 looks at how systems grow past one machine, and lesson 6 at what makes a system something people can run and change for years.

Each lesson ends with a lab: a small working model of the mechanism that you finish yourself, with tests that tell you when it works. The labs in this track are simulations in plain Kotlin that run in a second, with no Docker. The networking and operating systems tracks come next, because every later lesson assumes you know what a packet, a process and a system call are.

analogy: A system of record is like the bound ledger book in an old bank, and derived data like the cards the clerks keep on their desks: one card with today's totals per branch, a drawer of index cards that point from a customer's surname to the ledger page. The cards make questions fast. When coffee is spilled on one, a clerk rebuilds it by going through the ledger from the first page, and nobody ever corrects the ledger to match a card. The analogy breaks at speed. A clerk can't keep cards up to date with thousands of new ledger lines a second, so real systems update most derived data automatically on every write, and the hard part becomes the update that gets lost on the way.
in_your_world: In a payments platform the ledger is usually the system of record: an Oracle table of entries that are only ever appended. Almost everything else is a view of it: the Redis cache of merchant balances, the OpenSearch index support uses to find a payment by the last four digits of a card, the settlement file your batch job writes each night, and the warehouse finance queries. Kafka can play either role. If the payment service writes an event to Kafka and the ledger service builds its table from that topic, the topic is the source of truth and the Oracle table is derived. If the service commits to Oracle and a change-data-capture connector copies the changes into Kafka, it's the other way round. Know which one you have before an incident, because the recovery differs: a derived store is rebuilt from its source, and a source is restored from backups. And keep the morning refund report off the primary database. Point it at a replica or the warehouse, so a two-year scan never competes with authorizations.
mistake: The common mistake is treating a derived store as the truth: reconciling against the cache, fixing a wrong total in the reporting table by hand, or answering a dispute from the search index. It happens because the derived store is the one that is easy to see and query. When it disagrees with the system of record, the derived store is wrong by definition, and a hand-made fix is either overwritten at the next rebuild or, worse, kept and never explained. Fix the cause (the lost invalidation, the bug in the transform), then rebuild the view from its source. And make rebuilding a routine, tested operation rather than an emergency procedure: if you have never rebuilt a view from scratch, you don't know that you can.

compare.title: The same payments, two kinds of question

a.label: Operational
a.title: checkout, thousands of times a second
a.src:
-- one row, found through an index on its key, in milliseconds
SELECT status, amount_cents
FROM payments
WHERE payment_id = 'pay-0412233';

b.label: Analytical
b.title: an analyst, a few times a day
b.src:
-- every payment from two years, three columns of each
SELECT m.category,
       date_trunc('week', p.created_at) AS week,
       avg(CASE WHEN p.status = 'REFUNDED' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS refund_rate
FROM payments p
JOIN merchants m ON m.merchant_id = p.merchant_id
WHERE p.created_at >= now() - interval '2 years'
GROUP BY m.category, week
ORDER BY week, m.category;

compare.note: Both are SQL against the same tables, and one database will run both. The shape of the work is what differs. The first query follows an index to one row and returns in milliseconds. The second has to read every payment from two years, but only three of its columns, and its cost grows with the history. That's why it belongs on a copy laid out for scans, such as a warehouse or lakehouse table stored by column, and not on the database checkout is waiting for. The SQL track teaches the syntax, and the Storage engines track shows why the two layouts differ.

worked.title: Rebuild a materialized view from the log, by hand

steps.say: Start from the log: the seven records from the stepper, in order. A derived view may use nothing else.
steps.code:
0  pay-1  m-cafe   2026-03-02  AUTHORIZED  4000
1  pay-2  m-books  2026-03-02  AUTHORIZED  1250
2  pay-1  m-cafe   2026-03-02  CAPTURED    4000
3  pay-2  m-books  2026-03-02  CAPTURED    1250
4  pay-3  m-cafe   2026-03-02  AUTHORIZED   900
5  pay-3  m-cafe   2026-03-02  CAPTURED     900
6  pay-1  m-cafe   2026-03-03  REFUNDED    4000

steps.say: Name the question the view answers, and so its key. Daily totals answer "how much did merchant m take on day d?", so the key is (merchant, day) and the value is net cents.
steps.code: val totals = HashMap<Pair<String, String>, Long>()           // (merchant, day) -> net cents

steps.say: Decide what each kind of record does to the view. An authorization only reserves money, so it changes nothing. A capture adds on its own day; a refund subtracts on the day of the refund.
Rebuilding is clear, then replay from offset 0 in order. Clearing first is what makes it safe to run twice.
Check it against the live view. Same records, same order, same rules: the same answer, every time.

lab.title: Rebuild every view from the log
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 10 fail with `NotImplementedError`.

Read `Log.kt`. It's finished: `PaymentEvent` is one line of the log, `PaymentLog` appends lines to a file and replays them in order, `View` is the interface every derived view implements, and `PaymentService` writes to the log first and the views second.
In `Views.kt`, write `PaymentIndex.apply` and `get`. An authorization creates the entry; a capture or a refund changes only its status.
Write `DailyTotals.apply` and `total`: captures add, refunds subtract, authorizations do nothing.
Write `BalanceCache.get` and `apply`. A miss calls the loader and counts the load; an event for a merchant forgets that merchant's entry and no other.

Write `rebuild`, then run the tests until all 10 pass. `RebuildPropertyTest` uses jqwik, a property-testing library: it runs the same check against 40 random payment histories and, if one fails, shrinks it to the smallest history that still breaks.
hints: `byId[e.paymentId]?.let { byId[e.paymentId] = it.copy(status = e.kind) }` updates an existing entry and ignores an id it has never seen.
`totals.merge(e.merchant to e.day, delta, Long::plus)` adds `delta` to the value already there, or stores it if there is none.
`cached.getOrPut(merchant) { loads++; loader(merchant) }` runs the block only on a miss.
If `rebuilding twice does not count anything twice` fails, `rebuild` isn't clearing the views before it replays.

drill.title: Write rebuild from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `rebuild(log, views)` for a log that can replay its records in order and views that have `apply` and `clear`. Then write down the two things the log must guarantee for a rebuilt view to equal the live one.

recap: A data system is a few tools joined up by your code: a database keeps records, an index finds them, a cache reuses answers, a queue defers work and a batch job processes a lot at once.
The system of record holds each fact once and wins every disagreement. Everything computed from it (indexes, caches, totals, warehouses, models) is derived and can be rebuilt.
Write the system of record first and the views second, and keep the record complete and in order, so any view can be dropped and replayed.
Operational work touches a few records by key, in milliseconds, for your application. Analytical work scans millions of records, in seconds or minutes, for people asking new questions.

Warehouses, lakes and lakehouses answer where the analytical copy lives: a separate database, files on object storage, or files on object storage with an open table format that adds versions and atomic commits.

quiz.q: The fraud team keeps a Redis set of blocked card numbers, filled from the `blocked_cards` table in Oracle by a small job. Redis restarts and the set comes back empty. What should happen?
options: Restore the set from last night's Redis snapshot
Rebuild it from the `blocked_cards` table
Ask the fraud analysts to enter the blocked cards again
Nothing: the set refills itself as cards are used
quiz.why: The Redis set is derived from `blocked_cards`, so the table is the truth and the set is rebuilt from it. A snapshot of the copy is older than the table and would miss cards blocked since. The last option is the tempting one, because caches do refill on misses, but this set is checked for membership: an empty set doesn't miss, it just says every card is fine.

quiz.q: Which of these is operational work?
options: A merchant's dashboard showing their last 20 payments
Monthly refund rates per country for the board
Training a fraud model on two years of chargebacks
Finding which merchant categories grew fastest last quarter
quiz.why: The dashboard query is written into the application, runs every time a merchant opens the page, touches 20 rows of one merchant through an index, and has to answer in milliseconds. It looks like a report, which is the trap, but its shape is operational. The other three scan large parts of the history and can take minutes.

quiz.q: A team runs a two-year refund analysis on the primary payments database every morning at 10:00, and checkout response times jump every day at 10:00. What is the best fix?
options: Add an index on `status` so the analysis runs faster
Give the database server more CPU
Run the analysis on a separate copy: a read replica or the warehouse
Ask the team to run it at lunchtime, when traffic is lower
quiz.why: The analysis is analytical work: it reads every row from two years and competes with checkout's lookups for disk, memory and CPU. Moving it to a separate copy ends the competition for good. An index on `status` doesn't help a query that reads most rows anyway, and more CPU or a quieter hour only shrink the overlap until the data grows again.

quiz.q: A data lake holds the payments history as thousands of Parquet files in object storage. What does an open table format such as Iceberg add on top of them?
options: It converts the files into a faster format
It copies the data into a warehouse every night
It indexes every row so lookups by payment id take milliseconds
Metadata that lists which files make up each version of the table, with atomic commits
quiz.why: Iceberg leaves the Parquet files where they are and adds metadata files that describe each version of the table. A commit swaps a pointer to the new version in one step, so readers never see half a write, and old versions stay readable. It doesn't turn the lake into an operational database: fast lookups of one payment by key are still not what it's for.

quiz.q: The dashboard cache says merchant m-cafe has a balance of 49.00. The ledger says 9.00, because a 40.00 refund was recorded an hour ago. Which is right, and what do you do?
options: The cache, because it's what merchants see; correct the ledger
The ledger; evict the cache entry (or rebuild the cache) and find out why the refund never reached it
Neither; wait for tonight's settlement to decide
The cache, until the next batch job overwrites it
quiz.why: The ledger is the system of record, so it is right by definition and the cache is stale. Evicting the entry fixes this merchant now; finding the lost invalidation fixes the cause. Correcting the ledger to match a copy would turn a stale cache into lost money.

flashcards.back: It's computed from a system of record, so it can be deleted and rebuilt from the source without losing any fact. Indexes, caches, materialized views, warehouses and trained models are all derived.

flashcards.front: A derived copy disagrees with the system of record. Which is right?
flashcards.back: The system of record, always. The copy is stale or wrong, and gets fixed by rebuilding it from the source.

flashcards.front: Why write the log before updating the views?
flashcards.back: A crash between the two then leaves the views behind the log, which a rebuild fixes. The other order can leave a view holding a fact the log never recorded.

flashcards.front: OLTP vs OLAP, one line each?
flashcards.back: OLTP: application code reads and writes a few records by key, in milliseconds. OLAP: people scan millions of records to aggregate history, in seconds to minutes.
The stored result of a query, kept so the query doesn't have to run again. Net takings per merchant per day, built from the payment log, is one.

A lake is files of any format on object storage, with no tables or transactions. A lakehouse adds an open table format (Iceberg, Delta Lake) whose metadata makes those files tables with versions and atomic commits.

terms.plain: The store that holds the authoritative version of each fact; it wins any disagreement. Also called the source of truth.
Data computed from a system of record, such as an index or a cache. It can be thrown away and rebuilt.
A lookup table from a key to where its record is, so a read doesn't have to scan everything.
A saved copy of an answer that was expensive to compute, served until it goes out of date.
A list of jobs waiting to be done, so the code that creates work doesn't wait for it.
A program that processes a large, fixed set of input in one run, usually on a schedule.
Operational work (a few records by key, fast, for the application) and analytical work (scans of history, for people).
Files in open formats on object storage, plus a table format that gives them versions and atomic commits.

explain_back.prompt: A new colleague asks why your team keeps the same payment data in Oracle, Redis, OpenSearch and a warehouse, and whether that isn't asking for trouble. Explain it in your own words.
explain_back.answer: Only one of them is the truth. The Oracle ledger is the system of record: every payment is written there first, once, and it wins any argument. The other three are derived copies, each shaped for one kind of read. Redis answers the dashboard's "what's my balance?" in a millisecond, OpenSearch lets support search by card digits, and the warehouse lets analysts scan two years of history without slowing checkout down. The trouble is real: a copy can go stale or be wrong. We handle it by always writing the ledger first, keeping it complete and in order, and treating every copy as disposable. When one disagrees with the ledger, we fix the cause and rebuild the copy from the ledger, never the other way round.

deeper.body:
**One size doesn't fit all.** In 2005 Michael Stonebraker and Uğur Çetintemel argued in an ICDE paper, "One Size Fits All: An Idea Whose Time Has Come and Gone", that a single general-purpose database can't serve every workload well, and that specialized engines (for analytics, streams, search) would win in their niches. Twenty years on, that is the default architecture: one system of record and several specialized derived stores. The cost is the one this lesson names, keeping them in step, and Part IV of this course is about paying it well.

**A third kind of work.** Some analytical queries now run inside user-facing products: a merchant dashboard that shows payment volume per minute over the last 90 days, updated as payments arrive. Systems built for this (Apache Pinot, Apache Druid, ClickHouse) ingest events in real time and answer aggregates in tens of milliseconds, which classic warehouses, built for throughput on batch loads, don't. The Batch processing track compares engines.

**Data flows back too.** Analytical outputs often return to operational systems: a fraud model trained in the warehouse scores live payments, and a merchant risk tier computed overnight is copied into the database checkout reads. Pushing warehouse results back into operational stores is sometimes called reverse ETL. It's still derived data, just flowing the other way, and it needs the same care: a stale risk tier is a stale cache.

The framing of operational versus analytical systems, and of systems of record versus derived data, follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 1, which goes on to cloud versus self-hosted systems and to distributed versus single-node designs (lesson 5 of this track).
